subject: maths
title: Displaying data
summary: Learn to choose, draw and read column graphs, dot plots, stem-and-leaf plots, line graphs and pie charts, and to spot a graph that could mislead.
body:
Graphs turn a long list of numbers into a picture you can understand in seconds. News reports, sports apps and weather websites all use graphs to show what is going on. In this lesson you will learn which graph to use for which kind of data, how to draw it neatly, and how to read it carefully.

## Learning objective

By the end of this lesson you can choose, draw and read column graphs, dot plots, stem-and-leaf plots, line graphs and pie charts, and spot a graph that could mislead.

## Before you start

You need to know the difference between categorical and numerical data (from *Collecting and classifying data (Year 7)*), and how to find a fraction of an amount (from *Multiplying and dividing fractions (Year 7)*).

**Warm-up**

1. Find 1/4 of 360. *(Answer: 90)*
2. Find 12/30 of 360. *(Answer: 144, because 360 ÷ 30 = 12 and 12 × 12 = 144)*

## Think of it like this

### Choosing the right tool from a toolbox

A builder doesn't use a hammer for everything — a saw is for cutting and a screwdriver is for screws. Graphs are tools too. Column graphs compare groups, line graphs show change over time, and pie charts show parts of a whole. Pick the tool that fits the job.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a wrong tool usually just fails, but a wrong graph still "works" — it draws a picture, but the picture can give the reader the wrong idea.

## Key ideas

### Every graph needs the basics

A good graph has a **title**, labelled **axes** (with units if needed), an even **scale** that usually starts at 0, and a **key** if colours stand for something.

### Column graphs (categorical data)

A **column graph** uses separate bars, one per category, with gaps between them. The height of each bar is its frequency. Use it to compare categories, like favourite fruits.

### Dot plots (small sets of numerical data)

A **dot plot** has a number line, and each result is a dot stacked above its value. It shows the shape of the data at a glance. For example, goals scored in 12 games:

![A dot plot of goals scored in 12 games: 2 dots above 0, 3 dots above 1, 5 dots above 2, 1 dot above 3 and 1 dot above 4](/diagrams/y7/maths/displaying-data-dotplot.svg)

You can read straight off it: 2 goals happened most often (5 games), and there are 2 + 3 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 12 dots, one for each game.

### Stem-and-leaf plots (numerical data)

A **stem-and-leaf plot** splits each number into a **stem** (the tens digit) and a **leaf** (the ones digit). Leaves are written in order from smallest to largest. It keeps every actual value but still shows the shape, like a sideways column graph. Always include a key, such as "2 | 3 means 23".

### Line graphs (change over time)

A **line graph** plots values at different times and joins the points with straight lines. Time goes on the horizontal axis. A steeper line means a faster change; a line going down means a decrease.

### Pie charts (parts of a whole)

A **pie chart** is a circle split into **sectors**. Each sector shows a fraction of the whole. Because a full circle is 360°:

`sector angle = (frequency ÷ total) × 360°`

All the sector angles must add up to 360°.

### Shape, clusters and outliers

When you look at a dot plot or stem-and-leaf plot, describe its shape: where most values **cluster** (bunch together), any **gaps**, and any **outlier** — a value far away from the rest.

### Misleading graphs

A graph can trick the eye if its vertical axis doesn't start at 0, if its scale jumps unevenly, or if it has no labels. Always read the numbers, not just the bar heights.

![Two column graphs of the same sales, January 50 and February 52. On the left the axis starts at 48, so February's bar looks twice as tall as January's. On the right the axis starts at 0 and the bars look almost the same](/diagrams/y7/maths/displaying-data-misleading.svg)

## Worked examples

### Example 1

25 students chose their favourite fruit: apple 7, banana 4, mango 9, orange 5. Describe how to draw a column graph, and find how many more chose mango than banana.

![A column graph titled Favourite fruit of 25 students: apple 7, banana 4, mango 9, orange 5, with the vertical axis going up in 1s from 0 to 10](/diagrams/y7/maths/displaying-data-ex1.svg)

Step 1: put the categories (apple, banana, mango, orange) along the horizontal axis with a gap between bars — because the data is categorical.
Step 2: label the vertical axis "Number of students", going up evenly in 1s or 2s from 0 to at least 9 — so the tallest bar fits.
Step 3: draw each bar up to its frequency and add a title, such as "Favourite fruit of 25 students".
Step 4: compare mango and banana: 9 − 4 = **5 more students**.
Check: 7 + 4 + 9 + 5 = 25 students ✓

### Example 2

These are the ages of 11 people at a community bbq: 23, 12, 34, 28, 17, 41, 23, 30, 15, 36, 21. Draw a stem-and-leaf plot and find how many people are 30 or older.

Step 1: put the ages in order — so the leaves come out in order: 12, 15, 17, 21, 23, 23, 28, 30, 34, 36, 41.
Step 2: the stems are the tens digits 1, 2, 3, 4; write each ones digit as a leaf next to its stem.

| Stem | Leaf |
|---|---|
| 1 | 2 5 7 |
| 2 | 1 3 3 8 |
| 3 | 0 4 6 |
| 4 | 1 |

Key: 2 | 3 means 23 years.

Step 3: "30 or older" means the stems 3 and 4: 3 leaves + 1 leaf = **4 people**.
Check: count all leaves: 3 + 4 + 3 + 1 = 11 people ✓. The most common age is 23 (two leaves of 3 on stem 2).

### Example 3

30 students chose their favourite sport: football 12, netball 9, basketball 6, cricket 3. Find each sector angle for a pie chart.

Step 1: write each as a fraction of 30 and multiply by 360° — because the whole circle stands for all 30 students.
Step 2: football: 12/30 × 360° = 144°.
Step 3: netball: 9/30 × 360° = 108°; basketball: 6/30 × 360° = 72°; cricket: 3/30 × 360° = 36°.
Step 4: a quicker way: each student is worth 360° ÷ 30 = 12°, so multiply each frequency by 12°.
Check: 144° + 108° + 72° + 36° = **360°** ✓

![A pie chart of the favourite sport of 30 students: football 144°, netball 108°, basketball 72°, cricket 36°](/diagrams/y7/maths/displaying-data-ex3.svg)

## Common mistakes

- **Using a line graph for categories.** Joining "apple" to "banana" with a line means nothing. Fix: line graphs are for change over time; use a column graph for categories.
- **Unequal scales or not starting at 0.** This makes small differences look huge. Fix: go up in equal steps and start the vertical axis at 0.
- **Leaves out of order or missing a key.** Fix: order the leaves smallest to largest and always write a key like "2 | 3 means 23".
- **Using the frequency as the angle.** 12 students is not 12°. Fix: angle = frequency ÷ total × 360°.
- **Forgetting labels and titles.** Fix: before you finish, check title, both axis labels and units.

## Tips to remember

- **"Columns compare, lines show time, pies show parts."** A quick way to pick the graph.
- **Pie check: does it make 360?** If your angles don't add to 360°, something is wrong.
- **Degrees per person:** 360 ÷ total tells you how many degrees each person is worth.
- **Stem = tens, leaf = ones.** Picture a plant: the leaves grow off the stem, one leaf for each value. (A made-up memory trick.)
- **Read the axis before the bars.** If the axis doesn't start at 0, the bars can fool you.

## Key terms

- **Column graph** — a graph with separate bars showing the frequency of each category.
- **Dot plot** — a number line with a dot above each value for every result.
- **Stem-and-leaf plot** — a display that splits each number into a stem (tens) and a leaf (ones).
- **Line graph** — points joined by lines to show how something changes over time.
- **Pie chart** — a circle divided into sectors showing parts of a whole.
- **Sector** — a "slice" of a pie chart.
- **Outlier** — a value much bigger or smaller than the rest.
- **Scale** — the evenly spaced numbers along an axis.

## Summary

- Use column graphs for categorical data, dot plots and stem-and-leaf plots for numerical data, line graphs for change over time and pie charts for parts of a whole.
- Every graph needs a title, labelled axes and an even scale starting at 0.
- Stem-and-leaf plots keep every value: stem = tens, leaf = ones, leaves in order, with a key.
- Pie chart angle = frequency ÷ total × 360°, and all angles add to 360°.
- Read the numbers on a graph carefully — a cut-off axis can mislead.

questions.prompt: Which type of graph is best for showing how the temperature changed every hour during one day?
questions.explanation: A line graph shows how something changes over time, so it suits hourly temperatures. A pie chart shows parts of a whole, and the temperatures are not parts of anything.
steps: Ask what the graph needs to show: a change over time.
Line graphs are the tool for change over time (time on the horizontal axis).

mistakes.A: Step 1: pie charts show parts of one whole, but temperatures at different hours are not parts of a whole.
mistakes.C: Step 1: column graphs compare categories. Here the data changes over time.
mistakes.D: Step 1: a stem-and-leaf plot shows the spread of values, but loses the order of the hours.

questions.prompt: The dot plot shows the goals scored in each game of a season. How many games were played?
questions.explanation: Each dot is one game, so count all the dots: 2 + 3 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 12. The answer 5 is just the tallest stack (games with 2 goals).
steps: Each dot stands for one game.
Count every dot: 2 + 3 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 12 games.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 5 is only the dots above 2. Add the dots in every stack.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 4 is the largest number of goals on the axis, not the number of games. Count the dots.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 10 comes from adding the axis values 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4. Count the dots instead.

questions.diagram_alt: A dot plot of goals scored in each game: 2 dots above 0, 3 dots above 1, 5 dots above 2, 1 dot above 3 and 1 dot above 4

questions.prompt: In a stem-and-leaf plot, the key says "3 | 6 means 36". What value does the entry 4 | 7 stand for?
questions.explanation: The stem is the tens digit and the leaf is the ones digit, so 4 | 7 means 47. Writing 74 swaps the stem and leaf around.
steps: From the key, the stem is the tens digit and the leaf is the ones digit.
Stem 4 → 4 tens, leaf 7 → 7 ones, so 4 | 7 means 47.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the key shows 3 | 6 is 36, not 3.6, so the leaf is the ones digit, not tenths.
mistakes.B: Step 2: don't add the stem and leaf — put them side by side as tens and ones.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the stem (4) is the tens digit, so it comes first.

questions.prompt: In a class of 40 students, 10 said apple is their favourite fruit. What angle should the apple sector have in a pie chart?
questions.explanation: Apple is 10/40 = 1/4 of the class, and 1/4 of 360° is 90°. 10° uses the frequency as the angle, which ignores the total of 40.
steps: Write apple as a fraction of the class: 10/40 = 1/4.
A full circle is 360°.

mistakes.B: Step 3: the frequency is not the angle. Multiply the fraction 10/40 by 360°.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 25 is the percentage (25%). A pie chart angle is a fraction of 360°, not of 100.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the total is 40 students, not 100. Use 10/40, not 10/100.

questions.prompt: A stem-and-leaf plot (key: 3 | 1 means 31) shows: stem 3 → leaves 1 4 4 7; stem 4 → leaves 0 2 5; stem 5 → leaves 3 8; stem 6 → leaf 0. How many values are greater than 45?
questions.explanation: The values greater than 45 are 53, 58 and 60 — that is 3. The answer 4 also counts 45, but 45 is not greater than 45.
steps: "Greater than 45" does not include 45 itself.
Count 53, 58 and 60: 3 values.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 45 is equal to 45, not greater than it, so leave it out.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you counted everything from 40 up. Only values bigger than 45 count.
mistakes.C: Step 3: don't forget the stem 6 row — 6 | 0 means 60, which is greater than 45.

questions.prompt: The line graph shows the temperature at each hour from 9 am to 2 pm. Between which two times did the temperature rise the most?
questions.explanation: The rises are 4, 3 and 2 degrees, then it falls; the biggest rise is 21 − 17 = 4 °C, from 9 am to 10 am. 11 am to 12 pm leads to the hottest time, but that rise is only 2 °C.
steps: Find each change: 9→10 am +4, 10→11 am +3, 11 am→12 pm +2, 12→1 pm −1, 1→2 pm −3.
Rises are the positive changes; the steepest upward part of the line is the biggest rise.
The biggest rise is +4 °C, between 9 am and 10 am.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 12 pm is the hottest time, but the rise to it is only 26 − 24 = 2 °C. Compare the size of each rise.
mistakes.C: Step 2: from 1 pm to 2 pm the temperature falls by 3 °C — a fall, not a rise.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 24 − 21 = 3 °C, which is smaller than one of the other rises.

questions.diagram_alt: A line graph of temperature during the day: 9 am 17 °C, 10 am 21 °C, 11 am 24 °C, 12 pm 26 °C, 1 pm 25 °C, 2 pm 22 °C

questions.prompt: A stem-and-leaf plot (key: 3 | 1 means 31) shows: stem 3 → 1 4 4 7; stem 4 → 0 2 5; stem 5 → 3 8; stem 6 → 0. What is the difference between the largest and smallest values?
questions.explanation: The smallest value is 31 and the largest is 60, so the difference is 60 − 31 = 29. The answer 27 uses 58 as the largest, missing the last row 6 | 0.
steps: The smallest value is the first leaf on the first stem: 31.
The largest value is the last leaf on the last stem: 6 | 0 = 60.
Subtract: 60 − 31 = 29.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you subtracted the stems only (6 − 3). Use the full values, 31 and 60.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the largest value is in the last row: 6 | 0 means 60, not 58.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the smallest value is 31 (stem 3, leaf 1), not 30.

questions.prompt: The pie chart shows how 50 students travel to school. The bus sector has an angle of 72°. How many students catch the bus?
questions.explanation: 72° out of 360° is 72/360 = 1/5 of the circle, and 1/5 of 50 students is 10. The answer 20 is the percentage (20%), not the number of students.
steps: The sector is 72/360 of the whole circle.
Simplify: 72/360 = 1/5.
Find 1/5 of 50 students: 50 ÷ 5 = 10.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 72 is an angle in degrees, not a number of students. Find what fraction of 360° it is.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 360 ÷ 72 = 5 only tells you the fraction is 1/5. Now find 1/5 of the 50 students.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 1/5 is 20%, but the question asks for students. Find 1/5 of 50.

questions.diagram_alt: A pie chart titled How 50 students travel to school, with sectors for bus, car, walk and bike. Only the bus sector is marked: 72°

questions.prompt: The column graph shows drinks sold: Shop A sold 100 drinks and Shop B sold 95. The vertical axis starts at 90, so Shop B's column looks only half as tall as Shop A's. What fraction of Shop A's sales did Shop B really make?
questions.explanation: Use the real numbers: 95/100 = 19/20, so Shop B sold almost as much as Shop A. Judging by bar heights gives 1/2, but the bars are misleading because the axis starts at 90.
steps: Ignore the bar heights — the axis does not start at 0, so they mislead.
Use the real sales: Shop B ÷ Shop A = 95/100.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the bars look like 1/2 only because the axis starts at 90. Use the actual numbers.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 90 is where the axis starts, not Shop B's sales. Use 95.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 5/100 is the difference between the shops. Divide Shop B's sales by Shop A's.

questions.diagram_alt: A column graph titled Drinks sold: Shop A 100 and Shop B 95. The vertical axis starts at 90 and goes up in 2s to 100, so Shop B's column looks half as tall as Shop A's

questions.prompt: The line graph shows a plant's height each week. If the pattern in the weekly growth continues, what will its height be at week 5?
questions.explanation: The weekly growths are 2, 3, 4, 5 cm, going up by 1 each week, so next week it grows 6 cm: 18 + 6 = 24 cm. The answer 23 cm repeats last week's growth of 5 cm instead of continuing the pattern.
steps: The growth goes up by 1 cm each week, so in week 5 it grows 6 cm.

mistakes.B: Step 2: the growth is increasing each week, so it won't be 5 again — continue the pattern 2, 3, 4, 5, …
mistakes.C: Step 1: the height is not doubling (4 to 6 is not doubling). Look at the growth each week.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 4 cm was the growth in week 3. Find the next growth after 5 cm.

questions.diagram_alt: A line graph of a plant's height each week: week 0 is 4 cm, week 1 is 6 cm, week 2 is 9 cm, week 3 is 13 cm, week 4 is 18 cm. Week 5 is empty

questions.prompt: In a pie chart showing the favourite sports of 24 students, the soccer sector is 120°. Half as many students chose basketball as chose soccer. How many students chose basketball?
questions.explanation: Soccer is 120/360 = 1/3 of 24, which is 8 students, so basketball is half of 8 = 4 students. The answer 8 stops after finding the soccer students.
steps: Soccer's fraction of the circle: 120/360 = 1/3.
Soccer students: 1/3 of 24 = 8.
Basketball is half as many: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 students.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 60° is half of soccer's angle, not a number of students. Turn the angle into students first.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 8 is the number who chose soccer. Basketball has half as many.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 12 is half of all 24 students. Find the soccer students first, then halve that.

questions.prompt: Which set of data would be best shown in a stem-and-leaf plot?

options.B: The test marks (out of 50) of 25 students
options.C: The temperature at noon every day for a week, to show the trend
options.D: How a family spends its weekly budget, as parts of the total

questions.explanation: Test marks are numerical, and a stem-and-leaf plot shows their spread while keeping every mark. The temperature over a week is numerical too, but to show a trend over time you need a line graph.
steps: Stem-and-leaf plots are for numerical data where you want to see the spread and keep each value.
Colours are categorical; a budget split is parts of a whole (pie chart); a trend over time needs a line graph.
Test marks out of 50 suit a stem-and-leaf plot.

mistakes.A: Step 1: colours are categories, not numbers, so they have no stems or leaves. Use a column graph.
mistakes.C: Step 2: to show a trend over time, use a line graph — a stem-and-leaf plot loses the order of the days.
mistakes.D: Step 2: parts of a whole are best shown in a pie chart.
